items.title: OpenAI Quantifies the 'Jagged Frontier' of Coding Agents
items.summary: OpenAI's Research Acceleration report measures how far agents have moved into its own R&D workflow. Unaided success on tasks estimated at two to four human hours rose from 23% in March to 46% in October; on four-to-eight-hour tasks, from 13% to 35%. The shape is uneven: agents succeed at monitoring training runs (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), but only 35% of the time when launching runs and 25% when writing inference and serving code. More than two-thirds of researchers ran at least four agents concurrently by mid-October, and over 10% ran sixteen or more. Median API-list-price value of agent use hit $2,400 per researcher per day, up 62% from September, with the 90th percentile at $23,000. Researchers said they would give up 30% of team compute or 40% of headcount to keep the agents for three months. All figures are OpenAI's own estimates, with no outside audit.
items.impact: The most useful number is not the average but the gap: agents are strong at supervising existing systems and weak at building new ones, so the payoff still comes from narrow, well-specified work. The spend curve also reframes the economics of AI coding - the constraint is shifting from model capability to how much concurrent agent output a team can review and pay for.

items.title: Google Labs Opens Stitch Loop: an Agent That Maintains Software After Ship
items.summary: Google Labs opened a global waitlist for Stitch Loop, a long-running product agent that connects to a GitHub codebase and live product data through more than 180 integrations, custom MCP servers or local CLI uploads. It runs 'evergreen loops' in four steps - suggest, offer solutions, build in an isolated cloud sandbox and open a pull request, then reflect on live metrics. Three loops ship by default: security, latency and accessibility; teams can add custom goals such as checkout conversion. The security loop pairs Gemini 4 Carbon's cyber capabilities with CodeMender, DeepMind's autonomous code-security agent. Nothing merges without human review, and PRs can include screenshots and video. Stitch Loop can also serve as a context layer for other agents via its CLI and MCP, and works in Slack through @stitch. Google published no benchmarks, pricing or accuracy figures.
items.impact: Coding agents have mostly stopped at the merge; Stitch Loop targets the expensive tail of maintenance - vulnerabilities, slowdowns, accessibility debt - and turns it into a review queue. Moving from 'build this feature' to 'keep this metric healthy' is a meaningful shift in agent scope, though it also moves the bottleneck to human reviewers and raises the stakes on what production data an agent may read.

items.title: OpenAI's Performance Factory Runs 1,700 Codex Investigations in Three Months
items.summary: OpenAI detailed an internal system that keeps ChatGPT fast by putting Codex agents on performance regressions. When an alert fires, a Regression Workflow opens a task; a Codex agent investigates, records findings and proposes a fix that an engineer reviews and merges; after deployment, a second agent checks whether performance has returned to baseline. In just over three months the workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and identified root causes in over 600 cases - roughly 17 automated investigations a day. Engineers still approve every fix, though OpenAI says it is exploring letting agents handle that step too.
items.impact: This is one of the clearest published examples of agents doing continuous production engineering rather than one-off feature work: detect, diagnose, patch, verify. The closed loop with a verification agent is the part worth copying - it gives a measurable success signal instead of a plausible-looking patch. OpenAI's own next step, automating the approval gate, is exactly the boundary teams should think carefully about.

items.title: Humyn Labs Raises $47M to Build 'Gyms' That Train Humanoid Robots
items.source: There's A Robot For That / Business Standard
items.summary: Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, founded in 2026, raised $47 million: $26 million in equity led by Accel with Prosus Ventures, Jump Trading and Bajaj-linked funds, plus $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton. The company says it passed a $50 million annualised revenue run rate within six months by selling the real-world data humanoids need before they can do a job. It records people performing tasks in factories, warehouses, farms and homes, then converts that into training data spanning sight, sound, motion and touch for frontier labs, robotics firms and world-model developers in more than 20 countries; about 95% of customers are in the US. It plans dedicated robot gyms in Brazil, South Korea and India where models and hardware are tested in real conditions before deployment. Revenue and run-rate figures are company claims.
items.impact: Embodied AI's bottleneck is shifting from model architecture to the data and test infrastructure around it. Humyn's pitch - gyms as a service, not just labelled clips - treats deployment-time validation as a product, a pattern likely to repeat as more labs need physical tasks verified before a robot is trusted on a line.

items.title: Mitsubishi Electric Wires a Humanoid Into a CNC Cell via MCP and ROS
items.summary: At Japan's JIMTOF trade fair, Mitsubishi Electric demonstrated a work cell where a machine tool and a humanoid complete a machining job from a spoken instruction with no manual programming. An operator speaks the text to be engraved onto a tag; an AI planner using Mitsubishi's Maisart AI writes the machining program, talks to the CNC over the Model Context Protocol and to a Galaxea Dynamics humanoid over ROS, and the robot loads and unloads the workpiece. A second AI reviews every generated plan, and a person must still approve any action that changes machine settings or starts a cut. Mitsubishi says the technology could become practical around 2030, has not set a commercial launch, and notes humanoids are poorly suited to heavy workpieces.
items.impact: The notable move is giving the CNC controller an agent-like voice interface and making it the coordinator of a robot, rather than the other way around. MCP and ROS appearing together in one industrial loop shows agent protocols crossing from software into physical equipment - with a human approval gate still deliberately left in place.
